# 6. Cost (commit 17)

Generated by `docs/cost/cost_model.py` on 15 November 2026. Every number below comes from the tables in that script; change one and run it again to update this section. Prices are on-demand USD for Mumbai (ap-south-1) unless the table says otherwise, converted at ₹88 per dollar. Before quoting a figure outside this report, check it in the AWS Pricing Calculator (calculator.aws): AWS changes prices, and a few here are list prices from another region (marked).

## 6.1 The load we are pricing

On 28 April 2021, the day registration opened to everyone over 18, CoWIN took about 1.33 crore registrations [S1], 80 lakh of them between 4 and 7 pm, with a peak of 55,000 hits per second [S2], and sent 2.78 crore SMS [S4]. That gives the two rates we size for:

- **741 registrations/s**: the 4-7 pm average, $\frac{8\times10^{6}}{3\times3600}\approx741$.
- **475 registrations/s**: the lower end of the range in Sec 9.2, a less extreme opening day.

From the same day: about 74 hits per second for every registration per second ($\frac{55000}{741}$), and 2.1 SMS per registration. Outside the 3 busy hours the rest of the day averaged 70 registrations/s, 9% of the peak. Our model repeats that day shape: 3 hours at the peak, 21 hours at that lower level.

## 6.2 How many machines: from our own measurements

| What we measured | Result | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lookup service, 2 x t3.micro behind the ALB | 400 requests/s, p95 98 ms, 0 failed, never broke | commit 13, docs/evidence/13-load-lookup-* |
| Registration flow on one laptop process | 40 sign-ups/s (160 requests/s), p95 8 ms, did not break | commit 13, docs/evidence/13-load-registration-* |
| PostgreSQL, 4 shards of 1 CPU each | 1,731-1,813 sign-ups/s, p95 21-24 ms: about 450 per CPU | commit 16, docs/evidence/16-e6-* |
| Autoscaling under a spike (Kubernetes) | 2 to 8 pods, first new pod 31 s after the ramp began, 0 of 71,000 failed | commit 14, docs/evidence/14-e1-hpa-* |
| A server replaced by the Auto Scaling group | back to 2 healthy servers about 100 s after the stop | commit 15, docs/evidence/15-replace-* |

From those we take these working numbers (assumptions, kept on the safe side):

| Assumption | Value | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `req_per_server` | 300 | requests/s one c7i.large (2 vCPU) serves at the 60% CPU target. Two t3.micro (smaller, burstable) served 400/s without an error and we never found their limit, so 300 on a c7i.large is on the safe side |
| `regs_per_shard` | 600 | sign-ups/s per db.r6g.large shard (2 vCPU) at about 70% load; E6 measured about 450 per CPU at saturation |
| `min_shards` | 2 | shards kept even at low load, so losing one never stops everyone |
| `min_servers` | 4 | app servers kept running in Mumbai at any load, 2 per zone pair |
| `dr_servers` | 2 | warm standby app servers in Hyderabad |
| `resp_kb` | 3.0 | average response size in KB (our /centers answer is about 3 KB) |
| `new_conn_share` | 0.2 | share of requests that open a new connection (the rest reuse keep-alive) |
| `ops_month` | 300 | USD per month for CloudWatch, Route 53, backups, logs |
| `peak_hours` | 3 | busy hours per day, as on 28 April 2021 (4-7 pm) |
| `cloud_staff` | 2 | engineers to run the AWS setup (fewer than on-premises: no hardware), INR 20 lakh each per year |
| `busy_months` | 6 | months of campaign-level traffic in 3 years; the other 30 run at one tenth |

## 6.3 The infrastructure bill

Servers, databases, network and protection for a month in which every day peaks like 28 April 2021. That is the most a month could cost: the real campaign had a few days like that, not thirty. SMS is priced separately in 6.4 because it depends on the number of registrations, not on the machines.

| Component | 475 reg/s | 741 reg/s | Share at 741 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| app servers | $1,750 | $2,617 | 9% |
| database | $1,108 | $1,108 | 4% |
| cache | $252 | $252 | 1% |
| load balancers | $488 | $744 | 2% |
| WAF | $11,413 | $17,796 | 58% |
| data out | $5,084 | $7,797 | 25% |
| monitoring and DNS | $296 | $296 | 1% |
| **Per month, on-demand** | **$20,392** (₹17.9 lakh) | **$30,611** (₹26.9 lakh) | |
| Per month, 1-year commitments on the always-on part | $19,758 (₹17.4 lakh) | $29,976 (₹26.4 lakh) | |
| One such day | $717 (₹0.6 lakh) | $1,083 (₹1.0 lakh) | |

The largest item is WAF (58%). WAF charges per request inspected, so at 55,000 hits a second it costs more than the servers behind it. Inspecting only the API calls, and serving the page itself from a CDN, would cut it. App servers are a small share because the Auto Scaling group runs the peak fleet for 3 hours a day and a much smaller one the other 21. Commitments barely help for the same reason: most of the bill is the elastic part.

## 6.4 Cost per registration: SMS is most of it

| Per registration, at 741 reg/s | USD | INR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infrastructure (one peak day / registrations that day) | 0.000081 | 0.0072 |
| SMS, 2.1 messages via AWS local route [S13] | 0.00581 | 0.511 |
| SMS, 2.1 messages via an Indian DLT provider [S14] | 0.00356 | 0.314 |

**SMS is 99% of the cost of a registration.** For every 10 crore registrations: SMS ₹5.1 crore on AWS's route or ₹3.1 crore through a DLT provider, against about ₹7.2 lakh of infrastructure.

Two consequences:

- The per-mobile OTP limits from commit 12 save money, not just capacity. Without them, E4's single bot machine caused 1,200 SMS a minute; at $0.00278 each that is $200 an hour from one machine, and a botnet multiplies it.
- The SMS route matters more than any instance choice. AWS's default route to India is the international one, which costs about 25 times more [S13]; the DLT registration (sender ID and message templates) has to be done before launch.

## 6.5 Cloud or our own data centres?

On-premises has to be built for the peak all the time, in two places. The same peak, with N+25% spare per site and a second site for disaster recovery:

| | 475 reg/s | 741 reg/s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vCPUs needed at peak (app + databases with standbys + cache) | 256 | 388 |
| Servers (both sites) | 28 | 42 |
| Racks | 2 | 4 |
| Up front (servers, network) | ₹120.9 lakh | ₹166.4 lakh |
| Per month (racks, power, bandwidth, 3 engineers) | ₹11.4 lakh | ₹13.8 lakh |

Three years, infrastructure and the people to run it (SMS costs the same either way):

| | 475 reg/s | 741 reg/s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS + 2 engineers, campaign shape (6 peak months, then a tenth of the load) | ₹312.1 lakh | ₹394.3 lakh |
| AWS + 2 engineers, peak every day for 3 years | ₹745.9 lakh | ₹1,069.7 lakh |
| Own data centres + 3 engineers, 3 years | ₹531.7 lakh | ₹664.7 lakh |

For a campaign shaped like CoWIN's, busy for a few months and quieter afterwards, AWS costs about 59% of owning the hardware at 741 reg/s, with nothing to buy before the first registration and no hardware left over afterwards. If the busiest day really repeated every day for three years, owning would be cheaper (AWS at 161% of it): steady, predictable load at full size is where your own hardware pays off. The on-premises figures are on the low side: they use Dell's starting price, assumed network and staff costs, and no software licences, spares or hardware refresh, and buying and installing 42 servers in two cities takes months, not minutes.

## 6.7 What this estimate leaves out

- Static files (the web page, images) would be served from CloudFront and S3; small next to the rest.
- Taxes: AWS bills in India add 18% GST.
- People: the cloud version still needs engineers, but no one to replace disks or drive to a data centre.
- Prices change. The ALB, ElastiCache and WAF prices are from other regions' list prices and are close to, but not exactly, Mumbai's.
